---
title: "Regression models"
---

Why use regression for reading time? We could divide words into two groups and compare their average reading times. But predictability varies by degree, and word length, frequency, and passage context vary along with it. Regression gives us a way to ask how the distribution of reading time changes as these predictors change.

Okay. So what must we know before we write down a regression equation? We need four pieces of information: (i) what one row of the data represents, (ii) which measured quantity we want to explain, (iii) which measured quantities we will use to make the explanation more specific, and (iv) which aspects of the response distribution we allow to change. We will call these the **observational unit**, the **response**, the **predictors**, and the **regression target**, respectively. The names matter because a coefficient has no interpretation until all four have been fixed.

For instance, suppose a table contains one row for each word position. If the response is the average log reading time at that position and the predictor is word predictability, then the fitted relation compares word positions. Comparing individual readers would require rows that retain reader identities. We will return to this row question at the start of each new dataset rather than assuming that the answer carries over from one analysis to the next.

We will begin with the [Provo Corpus](https://osf.io/sjefs/), which records eye movements and predictability norms for words in short English passages ([Luke and Christianson 2018](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4)). The first table contains one row for each content word position, with eye movement measurements averaged across the readers who fixated that word. We therefore begin by defining the [Provo measurements](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data): what a first fixation is, what one row represents, and what was averaged.

This **aggregation across readers** turns the original reader and word observations into summaries for word positions. Those summaries let us make the regression calculations visible, but they no longer contain the variation among readers. We will keep track of that loss as we interpret each fitted model.

The basic regression idea builds directly on [expectation and variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd). We describe how the center of a response distribution changes with predictors, then ask how observations vary around that center. We begin with linear models for continuous responses, extend the same architecture to other response types with [generalized linear models](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd), and finally return to data containing repeated readers and items with [mixed models](structured-data.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: regression-index-data

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/content-word-positions.csv")
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)

regression_inventory <- data.frame(
  object = c(
    "content word positions",
    "passages",
    "parts of speech",
    "finite mean log first fixation durations"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(provo),
    length(unique(provo$Text_ID)),
    length(unique(provo$Word_POS)),
    sum(is.finite(provo$mean_log_ffd))
  )
)

regression_inventory
```

The opening regression question is visible in the observed Provo positions. Each point below represents one content word position within a passage after first fixation durations have been averaged across the readers who fixated that word. The blue curve is a descriptive smooth that helps us see how the response center changes before we choose a regression function.

```{r}
#| label: plot-regression-index-provo-overview
#| fig-cap: "Observed Provo word positions. The curve summarizes how mean log first fixation duration changes across modeled cloze surprisal before a regression function is chosen."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of modeled cloze surprisal against mean log first fixation duration for Provo word positions, with a gently rising blue smooth."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = 0.18, size = 0.7) + # dqr-allow: plot-aesthetic
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The response tends to rise with surprisal, though the curve also suggests that a straight line may be only an approximation. We begin by turning this visible pattern into a conditional mean and a fitted line, then check the restrictions introduced by that line.

A regression model specifies which parameter of a response distribution depends on which observed predictors, and through which function. The response distribution states which measurements are possible and how they vary; the regression function states how its parameters change across predictor values represented in the data.

The basic idea is easiest to see with a pair of predictions. Compare the fitted mean at a predictor value $x$ with the fitted mean at $x+1$. Their difference is the model's fitted change for one additional predictor unit. We next ask where such predictions come from, how uncertain they are, and what must be true for the contrast to answer the linguistic question we had in mind.

This specification assumes the earlier [estimator terminology](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd): an estimand is the target, an estimator is a random rule, and an estimate is its observed value. It also assumes that a [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) holds the observations fixed while comparing parameter values. We will briefly recall these objects whenever they do explanatory work.

## Linear regression

We begin with a [conditional mean](regression-models.qmd), restrict that mean to a line under [simple linear regression](simple-linear-regression.qmd), and then ask what the fitted line licenses through uncertainty, residual, and diagnostic calculations. Raw summaries for Provo word positions and fitted lines remain visible on the same response scale.

We introduce [multiple regression](multiple-regression.qmd) with MALD auditory
lexical decision items. These rows summarize retained correct trials and cannot
recover participant effects. With the MALD measurements fixed, we can ask how
to [code categories](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd), what happens when
[predictors correlate](correlated-predictors.qmd), how individual observations
[influence](influence.qmd) a fit, and how to represent [unequal
variance](heteroscedasticity.qmd). **Regularization** modifies a fitting
criterion to discourage coefficient values that the data support weakly;
[ridge regression](ridge-regression.qmd) develops that penalty.
[Interactions](interactions.qmd) use MegaOrientation's paired past and future
means to define differences among verb frame orientation shifts.

## Generalized response distributions

A Gaussian straight line mean is not appropriate for every linguistic response.
Binary choices, ordinal judgments, counts, and bounded sliders have different
supports and patterns of variation. [Generalized linear models](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd)
retain a predictor dependent parameter while changing the response family and
link. We therefore introduce each dataset when its measurement
scale requires a new family: SuperTelicity for Bernoulli models,
MegaVeridicality for ordered responses, Nettle and Storme for counts, and
MegaNegRaising for sliders that may attain their endpoints. In these population
fits, repeated participants and items remain outside the likelihood, so the
coefficients describe associations among the analyzed rows. The design of each
dataset adds a further interpretive constraint. MegaNegRaising verbs passed an
earlier acceptability screen; SuperTelicity records a temporal preposition
choice; MegaVeridicality records an ordered task response; and Nettle country
language totals become rates only after area enters as exposure.

## Repeated units

When we introduce [structured data](structured-data.qmd), we return to connected MALD trials and distinguish response rows from repeated listeners and spoken words. Random intercepts represent persistent modeled differences among sampled groups, while random slopes represent group variation in a predictor association.

We then combine repeated units with the earlier response families. A [logistic
mixed model](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd) represents repeated
SuperTelicity participants and items; an [ordinal mixed model](ordinal-mixed-models.qmd)
represents repeated MegaVeridicality respondents and verbs; and a [count mixed
model](poisson-mixed-models.qmd) represents paired French and English UCCA
passages while adjusting for passage length. For each analysis, we retain the
part of the source design needed to answer the current modeling question and
name the omitted terms before interpreting its coefficients.

To keep the observational unit visible, we record the analyzed row and the dependence retained or omitted in each dataset.

| Resource | Analyzed row | Response used here | Dependence or selection to remember |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Provo](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) | content word position within a passage | mean log first fixation duration across retained readers | reader variation was removed by aggregation; positions remain grouped by passage |
| [MALD](multiple-regression.qmd#mald-word-item-data) | word item or connected participant--word trial, depending on the analysis | log latency for correct trials | item summaries cannot recover listener effects; trial rows repeat listeners and words |
| [MegaOrientation](interactions.qmd) | participant judgment of a verb frame item | ordered orientation response | participants and verbs repeat; the descriptive analysis uses paired cell means |
| [SuperTelicity](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) | participant choice for one sentence item | *in* versus *for* | participants, verbs, and sentences repeat |
| [MegaVeridicality](ordinal-regression.qmd) | respondent judgment of one low-content verb sentence | *no*, *maybe*, or *yes* | respondents and verbs repeat; task samples were recruited separately |
| [Nettle](poisson-regression.qmd#nettle-country-counts) | country database record | reported language total | boundaries, cross-border languages, documentation, and regional history affect rows |
| [Storme](zero-inflated-counts.qmd) | morpheme--consonant--liaison combination | truncated normalized-frequency proxy | the value is derived from frequency rather than observed tokens under known exposure |
| [MegaNegRaising](bounded-responses.qmd) | participant slider response to one sentence | neg-raising or ease slider location | participants and verbs repeat; the balanced verbs passed an earlier acceptability screen |
| [French--English UCCA](poisson-mixed-models.qmd) | passage in one language | UCCA Scene count with node count as exposure | the two language rows for a passage form a pair |

For every dataset, we identify the response and repeated units, state the conditional target, fit on the observed support, show data and fitted values together, and evaluate the restrictions the model added. The [dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) records how the required concepts connect.

## Where the estimates come from

Some fitting rules have a closed form; others require an iterative calculation.
We will not treat a software call as the definition of an estimator. When a
closed form exists, we derive it from the stated loss or likelihood. When it
does not, we derive the quantity being optimized or integrated and then explain
the algorithm used to approximate the answer.

| Estimate | What is derived |
|---|---|
| [Simple OLS](frequentist-linear-regression.qmd#from-discrepancies-to-an-objective) | Differentiate squared error, solve the two normal equations, and obtain the slope and intercept formulas. |
| [Matrix OLS](design-matrices.qmd#from-squared-error-to-the-coefficient-estimates) | Expand the quadratic, compute its gradient, solve the normal equations, and state the full rank condition for a unique solution. |
| [Regression $t$](regression-t-statistic.qmd) | Standardize one coefficient estimate by its directly calculated standard error and derive its null distribution. |
| [Regression $F$](regression-f-statistic.qmd) | Compare the reductions in squared error from nested regressions and derive the resulting mean-square ratio. |
| [Bayesian regression](bayesian-linear-regression.qmd#from-likelihood-and-prior-to-posterior) | Complete the square, derive every posterior parameter, and compute the posterior from the observed Provo design. |
| [Ridge](ridge-regression.qmd#penalties-and-priors) | Differentiate the penalized objective and derive its equality with the posterior mode under a Gaussian coefficient prior. |
| [Logistic fitting](iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd) | Differentiate the Bernoulli log likelihood and derive the working response and weighted least squares update used by IRLS. |
| [Mixed model fitting](laplace-approximation.qmd) | Write the integrated likelihood and derive the local quadratic approximation used when the integral has no elementary solution. |

The ordinal, count, and ordered beta discussions likewise begin from each
observed row's likelihood contribution. Their coefficient estimates have no
general closed form, so the corresponding computation maximizes the displayed
likelihood numerically. This distinction matters: defining an estimator by its
objective is exact even when finding its numerical value requires an iterative
algorithm.

## Prerequisite map and learning targets

Linear regression uses [conditional expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd), [estimator properties](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd), and [confidence intervals](../statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd). Generalized linear models add response support, mean--variance relations, and link functions. Mixed models return to [independent sampling](../statistical-inference/independent-sampling.qmd): each additional row records another observation, whereas another participant or item requires another sampled unit.

After completing these discussions, students should be able to:

1. state the response, observational unit, repeated units, and conditional target before fitting a model;
2. justify a response family and link by naming their restrictions and an observable failure mode;
3. move from a likelihood or loss to an estimator, uncertainty statement, and interpretation on the response scale; and
4. distinguish an association among rows from a claim that generalizes across participants, items, passages, or languages.

Begin with [conditional means](regression-models.qmd), where the Provo response and predictor are connected without yet assuming a straight line.
